newsitem.title: UK: Record company denies Oasis to break up.
newsitem.headline: Record company denies Oasis to break up.

text.p: Record company executives on Friday denied reports that British pop superstars Oasis were to split up. But they confirmed Britain's top-selling band would not be touring in the "foreseeable future".
The band sparked speculation about a split after they abruptly cancelled a U.S. tour amid reports that brothers Liam and Noel Gallagher had come to blows.
Record company Creation said: "Unfortunately the band will not be touring in the foreseeable future, but in every other aspect Oasis will continue to exist and function as a band."
Oasis's record company Creation is 49 percent owned by Sony Music.
News of a possible split provoked a media frenzy in Britain, with tabloid newspapers devoting pages to the story. Television news bulletins also gave the story top billing.
The feuding brothers were spending time together getting over jetlag after flying back from America, Creation said, but a brief appearance for the media was planned next week.

Lead guitarist and songwriter Noel Gallagher flew home alone to London on Thursday evening, looking red-eyed and depressed. He refused to tell a barrage of reporters what was happening to the group that had helped lead a "Britpop" revival.

Singer Liam followed with the rest of the band on Friday morning, flying in from Atlanta where the tour ended so suddenly. But the singer, who normally trades insults with the media, also refused to answer a single question from reporters.
Oasis, whose first two albums have sold 20 million copies, were hailed as Britain's biggest pop phenomenon since the Beatles. A summer concert drew a record crowd of 250,000.
The bad boys of pop delighted in bad-mouthing the press and fellow stars. They let their music speak for them.

Some fans blamed the apparent breakup on Liam Gallagher's passionate affair with actress Patsy Kensit. They cast her as the villain of the pop soap opera, echoing the anger directed at Yoko Ono when the Beatles broke up in the Seventies.
Liam Gallagher had boasted: "We are bigger than Jesus. We will be as big as the Beatles, if not bigger."
But their concert tour of the United States had drawn mixed reviews in sharp contrast to the idolised Beatles, who never toured again after playing their last concert in San Francisco in 1966.
Liam and Noel Gallagher, the driving forces behind Oasis, had been sparring partners since childhood.
Acrimony and walkouts abounded once the group shot to fame and Noel was the first to admit to the pressures.
"You wanna try being me and Liam for an afternoon. You'd slit your own throat, mate," he said in a magazine interview last month.
